ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Lou Gehrig — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient with progressive weakness and loss of coordination: evaluation for a motor neuron disorder and its mimics, safety, and how he wants to receive results

text.paragraph: New patient with progressive weakness and loss of coordination: evaluation for a motor neuron disorder and its mimics, safety, and how he wants to receive results [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Over about a year he has lost strength and coordination, fumbles with buttons and a bat, trips on curbs, and fell on the ice in the winter, and he wants to know why. [S]
He has stopped playing and wants plain answers, delivered to him first. [S]
He wants to stay useful and to keep working in some form. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Henry Louis Gehrig was born on June 19, 1903, in the Yorkville section of Manhattan, New York, to Heinrich and Christina Gehrig, German immigrants. [D]

Three of his siblings died young: his sister Anna in September 1902 at about three months, his sister Sophie in the winter of 1906 of a combination of measles, diphtheria and bronchopneumonia, and a brother shortly after birth. [D]
He enrolled at Columbia University on a football scholarship in February 1921. [D]
He played first base for the New York Yankees and, on May 2, 1939, in Detroit, took himself out of the lineup after a then-record 2,130 consecutive games. [D]

In 1938 he batted .295, the first time under .300 since 1925, and his hitting fell off sharply in midsummer; he had an attack of lumbago and a badly jammed thumb that season. In the winter of 1938 to 1939 he lost his strength and collapsed while ice skating, in spring training 1939 he collapsed while putting on his uniform pants and his reflexes had slowed alarmingly, and at 35 he batted .143 in the first games of the 1939 season. [D]
His first neurological symptoms began in 1938, around the time of his 35th birthday. [D]
He had repeated head injuries, including concussions, during his playing career. [D]

text.paragraph: 5 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

text.paragraph: No medications started by this date.

Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, quiet and courteous; frustrated and worried by his loss of strength; PHQ-2 1. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

tr.td: Progressive weakness and loss of coordination for about a year: fumbling with buttons and a bat, tripping on curbs, a fall on the ice in the winter, muscle cramps and twitching in the arms and thighs; no numbness, pain, double vision, or trouble speaking or swallowing. Examination: wasting of the hand muscles (left more than right), fasciculations in both arms and thighs, weakness of grip and of left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and a positive Hoffmann sign, normal sensation. Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs; evaluation for motor neuron disease and its mimics begun, with neuromuscular neurology consultation booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented decline in 1938 and 1939; superseded by the diagnosis.

list.item: Progressive weakness and loss of coordination for about a year: fumbling with buttons and a bat, tripping on curbs, a fall on the ice in the winter, muscle cramps and twitching in the arms and thighs; no numbness, pain, double vision, or trouble speaking or swallowing. Examination: wasting of the hand muscles (left more than right), fasciculations in both arms and thighs, weakness of grip and of left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and a positive Hoffmann sign, normal sensation. Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs; evaluation for motor neuron disease and its mimics begun, with neuromuscular neurology consultation booked: active, confirmed [S]

Evaluation of progressive weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs: blood count, metabolic panel with calcium, creatine kinase, vitamin B12, TSH, A1c, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, and an HIV test; MRI of the brain and cervical spine; seated spirometry. Guideline: Practice parameter update: the care of the patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: multidisciplinary care, symptom management, and cognitive/behavioral impairment (an evidence-based review) (2009); A proposal for new diagnostic criteria for ALS (Gold Coast criteria) (2020); El Escorial revisited: revised criteria for the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (2000) [S]

Neuromuscular neurology consultation with EMG and nerve conduction studies for progressive weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. Guideline: Practice parameter update: the care of the patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: multidisciplinary care, symptom management, and cognitive/behavioral impairment (an evidence-based review) (2009); A proposal for new diagnostic criteria for ALS (Gold Coast criteria) (2020) [S]

Safety while the evaluation proceeds: no competitive play or heavy lifting, a physical therapy assessment of balance and gait, home fall precautions (night lights, rails, no loose rugs), and a same-day call for any trouble swallowing or breathing; results given to him first, in person. Guideline: Practice parameter update: the care of the patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: multidisciplinary care, symptom management, and cognitive/behavioral impairment (an evidence-based review) (2009) [S]
Referral to neurology (neuromuscular), Priscilla Nakamura, MD, ordered 1939-05-04 [S]
